practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following describes the 'plum pudding' model of the atom?
A) A tiny, dense nucleus surrounded by electrons in fixed energy levels
B) A positively charged sphere with electrons embedded throughout it
C) A solid, indivisible sphere with no internal structure
D) A nucleus containing protons and neutrons with electrons orbiting freely
practice_questions.marks: B) A positively charged sphere with electrons embedded throughout it [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the name of the experiment that provided evidence for the nuclear model of the atom, and who carried it out.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The Geiger–Marsden (gold foil / alpha scattering) experiment (1) carried out by Geiger and Marsden under Rutherford's direction / by Rutherford (1).
Secure: Names gold foil experiment and Rutherford.
Developing: Names either the experiment or the scientist.
Emerging: No creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happened in the gold foil experiment and explain what this showed about the structure of the atom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Most alpha particles passed straight through (1) showing the atom is mostly empty space; a small number were deflected at large angles (1) showing there is a concentrated positive charge at the centre; this tiny, dense centre is the nucleus (1).
Secure: Two observations with correct interpretation.
Developing: States particles passed through or were deflected but does not fully interpret.
Emerging: Vague description of the experiment.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the development of the atomic model from Dalton to Bohr is an example of how scientific knowledge develops over time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Each model was accepted as the best explanation of available evidence at the time (1); Dalton's solid sphere was replaced when Thomson discovered electrons (1); Thomson's plum pudding was replaced when Rutherford's alpha scattering results could not be explained by a diffuse positive charge (1); Bohr modified Rutherford's model when it could not explain why electrons didn't lose energy and spiral inward (1); models are revised only when new evidence forces revision — they are not discarded arbitrarily (1).
Secure: Four points with clear sense of evidence driving change.
Developing: Two to three changes described with partial explanation.
Emerging: Names scientists without explaining the process.

practice_questions.text: Compare the Rutherford nuclear model and the Bohr model of the atom. What problem did Bohr's model solve that Rutherford's could not?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both models have electrons orbiting a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (1); Rutherford's model does not specify where electrons can orbit (1); Bohr proposed electrons occupy fixed energy levels (shells) and do not emit energy within a level (1); this solved the problem of why electrons don't spiral into the nucleus under classical physics (1).
Secure: Three points with correct comparison.
Developing: Describes one model adequately.
Emerging: Names both models without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain how James Chadwick's discovery of the neutron in 1932 completed the nuclear model of the atom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Before 1932, the nucleus was thought to contain only protons (1); the mass of most atoms was greater than could be explained by protons alone (1); Chadwick discovered a neutral particle (the neutron) with a mass similar to a proton, which accounted for the extra mass and completed the picture of the nucleus containing both protons and neutrons (1).
Secure: Problem and solution both addressed.
Developing: States neutron was discovered and adds to nucleus but does not explain the mass problem.
Emerging: Names neutron without explaining its significance.

before.exam_tip_html: Questions on the history of atomic models almost always ask you to explain the change — not just name the new model, but say what evidence forced the revision. For example, “Rutherford’s nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model because most alpha particles passed straight through (showing the atom is mostly empty space) but a small number were deflected at large angles (showing a dense, concentrated positive charge at the centre).” Naming the result is worth one mark; explaining what it means for atomic structure is worth the rest. Dates are commonly tested: Dalton 1803, Thomson 1897, Rutherford experiment 1909 (published 1911), Bohr 1913, Chadwick 1932.
before.content_html:
A Model That Keeps Changing

The history of atomic theory is a textbook case of how science actually works: each model served well until new experimental evidence forced scientists to revise or abandon it. No single scientist “discovered” the atom in its modern form — the picture we use today was built up over more than a century, with each breakthrough depending on the tools and questions of its time. Understanding this story helps you think like a scientist, not just remember facts.

Key Fact

The atomic model developed in stages: Dalton (solid sphere) → Thomson (plum pudding) → Rutherford (nuclear model) → Bohr (electron shells) → Chadwick (neutron discovered). Each change was driven by new experimental evidence, not by theory alone.

Dalton’s Solid Sphere (1803)

John Dalton proposed that all matter is made of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms. In his model, atoms were like tiny solid spheres — different for each element, but impossible to break apart. Dalton’s theory was based on careful measurements of the masses of reactants and products in chemical reactions (the law of definite proportions and the law of multiple proportions). At the time, it was the best explanation for why elements combine in fixed ratios.

Thomson’s Plum Pudding Model (1897)

In 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron by experimenting with cathode rays — beams of particles that travelled from the negative terminal of a tube towards the positive terminal in a vacuum. He showed these particles had a negative charge and a mass far smaller than any atom. This proved that atoms were not indivisible — they contained smaller parts.

Thomson proposed the plum pudding model: the atom is a sphere of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it, like plums in a pudding. The positive charge was spread evenly throughout the sphere. This model explained why atoms were electrically neutral overall.

Rutherford’s Nuclear Model (1911)

The plum pudding model was overturned by a famous experiment. Working in Manchester, Ernest Rutherford directed Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden to fire alpha particles at a very thin sheet of gold foil (the Geiger–Marsden experiment, 1909; Rutherford’s interpretation published 1911). According to the plum pudding model, the alpha particles should have passed straight through with minimal deflection — positive charge was spread out, so it could not exert a strong force.

Most alpha particles did pass straight through the gold foil — suggesting that most of the atom is empty space. However, a small number were deflected at large angles, and a very few bounced almost straight back. Rutherford famously described this as “almost as incredible as if you fired artillery shells at tissue paper and they came back and hit you.”

The only explanation consistent with these results was that almost all the mass of the atom, and all its positive charge, was concentrated in an extremely small, dense region at the centre: the nucleus. The electrons orbit this nucleus, and most of the atom is empty space between the nucleus and the electrons. This replaced the plum pudding model.

Bohr’s Shell Model (1913)

Rutherford’s model had a problem: electrons orbiting a nucleus should, according to classical physics, lose energy and spiral into the nucleus. The atom should be unstable. Niels Bohr solved this by proposing that electrons do not orbit freely — they can only exist in specific energy levels (called shells or orbits). Electrons can move between levels by absorbing or emitting energy, but within a level they do not radiate energy. This explained the stability of atoms and also accurately predicted the spectrum of light emitted by hydrogen atoms.

Key Fact

Bohr’s key addition was that electrons occupy fixed energy levels (shells). Electrons can jump to a higher shell by absorbing energy and drop to a lower shell by emitting energy (as light). This is why each element produces a unique spectrum of light.

Chadwick and the Neutron (1932)

One loose end remained: the mass of atoms was always greater than could be accounted for by protons alone. In 1932, James Chadwick bombarded beryllium with alpha particles and detected a previously unknown neutral particle with a mass similar to a proton. He had discovered the neutron. This completed the picture of the nucleus as containing both protons and neutrons, explaining why atoms of the same element can have different masses (isotopes).

Each model in this story was the best available explanation of the evidence at the time. No model was abandoned because someone decided it was wrong — each was replaced only when new experimental evidence (cathode rays, alpha scattering, emission spectra, neutron bombardment) could not be explained by the existing model. This is how science should work: models are provisional and open to revision. The fact that today’s atomic model is also more complex than Bohr’s (electrons are described as probability clouds, not fixed orbits) shows that the process continues.

practice_questions.text: Explain why reactivity increases going down Group 1 (the alkali metals).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Going down the group, the outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus (1); there are more inner shells, increasing shielding of the outer electron from the nuclear attraction (1); therefore the outer electron is more easily lost, making the atom more reactive (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare the properties of transition metals with those of Group 1 metals. Give at least four differences.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Transition metals have higher melting points than Group 1 metals (1); they are harder and denser (1); they are much less reactive (1); they form coloured compounds and can have variable oxidation states (1); they can act as catalysts (accept any four from this list).
Secure: Three differences correctly stated.
Developing: Two differences.
Emerging: One correct property.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Mendeleev's periodic table provides an example of how scientific models gain credibility.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic weight and identified patterns of similar properties (1); he left deliberate gaps where no known element fitted (1); he predicted the properties of these missing elements (1); when elements were discovered with properties matching those predictions (e.g. gallium and germanium), the model was confirmed (1); making testable predictions that are subsequently verified is a key way that a scientific model gains acceptance (1).
Secure: Four points with clear connection to model credibility.
Developing: Describes predictions and discovery but does not connect to scientific process.
Emerging: Names Mendeleev with limited development.

practice_questions.text: Chlorine water is added to separate solutions of potassium bromide and potassium iodide. Predict and explain what you would observe in each case.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Potassium bromide: solution turns orange/brown (1) because chlorine displaces bromine (1) as chlorine is more reactive than bromine (1). Potassium iodide: solution turns brown/dark (1) because chlorine displaces iodine (1) as chlorine is more reactive than iodine (1).
Secure: Both correct observations with correct displacement explanation.
Developing: One correct with explanation, one vague.
Emerging: One correct observation without explanation.

before.content_html:
A System That Predicts Behaviour

The periodic table is one of the most powerful tools in chemistry. It does not just list the elements — it organises them so that patterns in their properties become visible and predictable. A chemist encountering an unfamiliar element for the first time can look at its position in the table and make reasonable predictions about its reactivity, the type of bonds it is likely to form, whether it is a metal or non-metal, and even what formula its compounds might take. Understanding why those predictions work requires knowing how electrons are arranged in atoms: the structure of the outer electron shell is the key to an element’s chemical behaviour.

How the Periodic Table Is Organised

Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number (number of protons). The table is divided into horizontal rows called periods and vertical columns called groups. Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, which is why they share similar chemical properties.

Key Fact

The periodic table organises elements by atomic number. Periods (rows) share the same number of electron shells. Groups (columns) share the same number of outer electrons and therefore have similar chemical properties. Metals appear on the left; non-metals on the right.

Mendeleev and the Predictions of the Table

Mendeleev published his periodic table in 1869, arranging elements by atomic weight (not atomic number, as we use today) but grouping elements with similar properties in the same columns. Where no known element fitted, he left a deliberate gap and predicted the specific properties of the missing element — including its expected density, melting point, and the formula of its oxide. When gallium was discovered in 1875 and germanium in 1886, their measured properties closely matched his predictions. This predictive success led to wide scientific acceptance of his table and is a powerful example of how a scientific model gains credibility through making accurate, testable predictions about phenomena not yet observed.

Group 1 — The Alkali Metals

The alkali metals (Group 1: lithium, sodium, potassium, and below) each have one electron in their outer shell. They are soft metals with relatively low melting points, and they react vigorously with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas:

$$2Na + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_2$$

Going down Group 1, reactivity increases. This is because the outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and is more shielded from the nuclear attraction by inner electron shells. It is therefore more easily lost. The elements also become denser and have lower melting points going down the group.

Group 7 — The Halogens

The halogens (Group 7: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine) each have seven electrons in their outer shell. They exist as diatomic molecules (\(Cl_2\), \(Br_2\), \(I_2\)) and are highly reactive non-metals that react with metals to form ionic salts called halides.

Going down Group 7, reactivity decreases. The outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is harder to attract an extra electron to complete the shell. A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt: for example, chlorine water added to potassium bromide solution turns the solution orange, as bromine is released.

Key Fact

Group 1: reactivity increases down the group (outer electron further from nucleus, more shielded, more easily lost). Group 7: reactivity decreases down the group (outer shell further from nucleus, harder to gain an extra electron). These trends are opposite because metals lose electrons while non-metals gain them.

The noble gases (Group 0: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon) have completely full outer electron shells. This makes them very stable and extremely unreactive — they rarely form compounds under normal conditions. Boiling points increase going down the group. Noble gases are used where unreactive conditions are needed: argon in welding (shields the weld from oxygen), helium in balloons and airships, neon in lighting.

The transition metals occupy the central block of the periodic table. Compared with Group 1 alkali metals, they are much less reactive, harder, denser, have higher melting points, and are much better at acting as catalysts. A key distinguishing feature is that transition metals form coloured compounds (copper compounds are blue or green; iron(II) compounds are pale green; iron(III) compounds are orange-brown) and can often form ions with more than one charge (e.g. iron as Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺).

Familiar examples: iron (Fe) as a catalyst in the Haber process for ammonia; copper (Cu) as an electrical conductor; titanium (Ti) in aircraft and biomedical implants; nickel (Ni) in catalytic converters. Transition metals are useful precisely because they are less reactive than Group 1 metals, yet still able to participate in chemical reactions as catalysts.

Metallic — positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons [1], held by electrostatic attraction between ions and electron sea [1], conducts in all states because delocalised electrons are always free to move [1]. Secure: four points with correct reasoning. Developing: three points.

before.exam_tip_html: For 4-mark compare-or-contrast questions on bonding, always give a named example for each bond type and link the bond to at least one property. For the 6-mark extended-response question on metallic bonding, structure your answer around the sea of delocalised electrons — explain what it is, then use it to account for conductivity, malleability and high melting point separately. Avoid saying aluminium 'rusts' — this is a common error flagged in examiner reports.

before.content_html:
Conservation of Mass

In any chemical reaction, atoms are neither created nor destroyed — they are simply rearranged. This is the law of conservation of mass. It means a correctly written symbol equation must have the same number of each type of atom on both sides of the arrow. An equation with unequal atom counts is unbalanced and does not represent a real reaction.

Key Fact

In a chemical reaction, total mass is conserved. A balanced symbol equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides of the arrow. You balance equations by adding large numbers (coefficients) in front of formulas — never by changing the subscripts inside a formula.

Balancing Symbol Equations

To balance a symbol equation, count the atoms on each side and adjust the large numbers (coefficients) in front of formulas until both sides match. You must never change the subscripts inside a formula (that would change the substance itself). Work through one element at a time, leaving hydrogen and oxygen until last when they appear in water or acids.

Balance the equation for the combustion of propane: \(C_3H_8 + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + H_2O\)

Step 1: Count carbons. Left: 3; Right: 1. Put a 3 in front of \(CO_2\):
\(C_3H_8 + O_2 \rightarrow 3CO_2 + H_2O\)

Step 2: Count hydrogens. Left: 8; Right: 2. Put a 4 in front of \(H_2O\):
\(C_3H_8 + O_2 \rightarrow 3CO_2 + 4H_2O\)

Step 3: Count oxygens. Right: 3×2 + 4×1 = 10. Left needs 5 \(O_2\):
\(C_3H_8 + 5O_2 \rightarrow 3CO_2 + 4H_2O\)

Step 4: Check all atoms. C: 3=3 ✓ H: 8=8 ✓ O: 10=10 ✓. The equation is balanced.

State symbols can be added in brackets after each formula to show the physical state: (s) = solid, (l) = liquid, (g) = gas, (aq) = aqueous (dissolved in water). For example: \(Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow MgCl_2(aq) + H_2(g)\)

Relative Formula Mass

The relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of a compound is calculated by adding together the relative atomic masses (\(A_r\)) of all the atoms shown in its formula. For example, for water (\(H_2O\)):

$$M_r(H_2O) = 2 \times A_r(H) + 1 \times A_r(O) = 2 \times 1 + 16 = 18$$

For sulfuric acid (\(H_2SO_4\)): \(M_r = 2(1) + 32 + 4(16) = 98\). You need the periodic table to look up \(A_r\) values. The relative formula mass tells you the mass of one formula unit in atomic mass units, and is numerically equal to the mass of one mole in grams.

Key Fact

Relative formula mass (Mr): add up the Ar of every atom in the formula, accounting for subscripts. Mr of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + 3×16 = 100. No units — it is a ratio relative to ¹²C.

The Mole

Atoms and molecules are far too small to count individually, so chemists use the mole as a counting unit. One mole of any substance contains the same enormous number of particles — approximately \(6.02 \times 10^{23}\) — known as Avogadro's constant. The genius of the mole is that one mole of an element has a mass in grams exactly equal to its relative atomic mass.

The key equation linking moles, mass, and molar mass is:

$$\text{number of moles} = \frac{\text{mass (g)}}{\text{molar mass (g/mol)}}$$

Rearranged: mass = moles × molar mass, or molar mass = mass ÷ moles.

Worked example: How many moles are in 44 g of carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\), \(M_r = 44\))?
Moles = 44 ÷ 44 = 1 mol.

Second example: What mass of sodium hydroxide (NaOH, \(M_r = 40\)) is needed to make 0.5 mol?
Mass = 0.5 × 40 = 20 g.

Always show your working in full and include units at every step — examiners deduct marks for missing units on multi-step calculations.

Using Equations to Calculate Reacting Masses

A balanced symbol equation shows the molar ratios of reactants and products — the large numbers (coefficients) tell you how many moles of each substance react. Combined with molar masses, this allows calculation of the mass of any reactant or product from a known mass of another.

Calculate the mass of iron produced when 160 g of iron(III) oxide (\(Fe_2O_3\)) reacts with excess carbon:
\(2Fe_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Fe + 3CO_2\)

Step 1: Find \(M_r\) of \(Fe_2O_3\): \(2 \times 56 + 3 \times 16 = 160\) g/mol.

Step 2: Calculate moles of \(Fe_2O_3\): \(\frac{160}{160} = 1 \text{ mol}\).

Step 3: Use the molar ratio. From the equation, 2 mol \(Fe_2O_3\) → 4 mol Fe, so 1 mol \(Fe_2O_3\) → 2 mol Fe.

Step 4: Convert moles of Fe to mass: \(2 \times 56 = \mathbf{112 \text{ g}}\).

Key Fact

Reacting mass calculation (Higher): (1) write balanced equation, (2) calculate Mr of known substance and find moles, (3) use molar ratio from equation to find moles of unknown substance, (4) convert moles to mass. Always show every step and include units.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Conservation of mass means balanced equations must have identical atom counts on both sides. Balance by adjusting coefficients, never subscripts.
  • Relative formula mass (Mr) is the sum of all relative atomic masses in a formula. One mole of a substance has a mass in grams equal to its Mr.
  • Avogadro's constant (≈ 6.02 × 10²³) is the number of particles in one mole. Higher Tier: moles = mass ÷ molar mass; use molar ratios from balanced equations to calculate reacting masses.

practice_questions.text: A scientist finds that when 2.4 g of magnesium burns in air, a white solid with a mass greater than 2.4 g is produced. Zinc oxide reacts with carbon to produce zinc and carbon dioxide:
2ZnO + C → 2Zn + CO₂
(Ar: Zn = 65, O = 16, C = 12)
Calculate the mass of zinc produced from 18.1 g of zinc oxide, and explain what the molar ratio in the equation tells you about the reaction.

Secure: four calculation marks. Developing: correct Mr and moles only.

flashcard_questions.a: A unit of amount of substance. One mole contains approximately 6.02 × 10²³ particles and has a mass in grams equal to the relative formula mass.
The number of particles in one mole of any substance, approximately 6.02 × 10²³.
Number of moles = mass (g) ÷ molar mass (g/mol).

flashcard_questions.a: The physical state of each substance: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water.
